core: what exploratory data analysis is — the open-ended first look at data before formal modeling, attributed to John Tukey's framing
goals of EDA: spot errors, understand ranges and shapes, notice patterns, generate questions
tools of exploration: summary numbers (minimum, maximum, average, typical value, spread) and simple charts (histograms, scatter plots)
EDA versus confirmatory analysis: exploration finds hypotheses, confirmation tests them
what EDA is not: not proof, not cherry-picking (honesty principle)
supporting: history of EDA: Tukey's 1977 book Exploratory Data Analysis as the seminal work
the role of graphics in EDA
common analysis questions EDA is used to answer
outOfScope: chart design and visualization technique (visualization sibling topic)
prediction and model building (prediction sibling topic)
outlier treatment and detection methods (outliers sibling topic)
formal statistical tests and hypothesis-testing machinery (confirmatory analysis, taught only as a contrast)

claims.claim: Exploratory data analysis (EDA) is an approach or philosophy of data analysis, not a fixed bundle of techniques: it postpones assumptions about what kind of model the data follow and lets the data itself reveal underlying structure.
John Tukey's 1977 book Exploratory Data Analysis is the seminal work that established the EDA approach.

In the EDA sequence the analysis comes before the model — Problem, Data, Analysis, Model, Conclusions — whereas classical analysis imposes a model before analyzing; EDA's goal is to infer what model, if any, would be appropriate.

Common questions EDA is used to answer include what a typical value is, how the values spread, what shape the data takes, and whether variables relate to each other; the scatter plot is a broad-brushed technique that applies almost universally.
EDA relies heavily on simple graphical techniques such as histograms and scatter plots, which NIST describes as the shortest path to insight into a dataset.

Exploring numerical data combines summary statistics (mean, median, minimum, maximum, measures of spread such as the standard deviation) with visualizations; box plots reach to the minimum and maximum values, and the median and quartiles give a robust sense of the typical value and spread.
The primary goal of EDA is to maximize the analyst's insight into a dataset and its underlying structure, including detecting patterns and understanding what is and is not in the data.

Tukey argued that exploration and confirmation are both needed: ideas come from previous exploration, finding the question is often more important than finding the answer, and analysts should avoid multiplicity — patterns found by hunting through many possibilities can be coincidental, so exploratory findings need confirmatory testing.

conflictingEvidence.issue: Is EDA a set of techniques or an attitude?
positions: The NIST e-Handbook notes most EDA techniques are graphical and catalogs specific techniques such as histograms, scatter plots, and box plots.
Tukey (1980) insists EDA is an attitude, a flexibility, and a reliance on display, NOT a bundle of techniques.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: Both sources agree simple graphics are central to EDA. The lesson teaches EDA as an open-minded approach that leans heavily on basic summary numbers and charts, which satisfies both framings.

conflictingEvidence.issue: Can a pattern noticed during exploration be reported as a result?
positions: Informal practice sometimes reports explored patterns directly as findings.
Tukey (1980) warns analysts to randomize and avoid multiplicity, and the NIST e-Handbook separates the analysis-first EDA sequence from the formal testing of classical analysis.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson states that exploration generates hypotheses that require confirmatory testing before they count as findings, and treats direct reporting of an explored pattern without confirmation as cherry-picking.

rightsIssues: NIST e-Handbook pages are U.S. government works; used as REFERENCE_ONLY with original prose only.

Tukey 1980 is a copyrighted journal article (The American Statistician); the abstract was read via an Internet Archive capture of the Taylor & Francis page and used as REFERENCE_ONLY — no wording reproduced beyond the factual gist.

sourceRecords.title: NIST/SEMATECH e-Handbook of Statistical Methods — 1.1.1. What is EDA?
sourceRecords.notes: Read live 2026-08-21. States that EDA is an approach/philosophy that postpones assumptions about the model and lets the data reveal underlying structure; names Tukey's 1977 book Exploratory Data Analysis as the seminal work; describes EDA's main role as open-minded exploration. Supports the definition, the Tukey attribution, and the 'not a bundle of techniques' framing.

sourceRecords.title: NIST/SEMATECH e-Handbook of Statistical Methods — 1.1.2. How Does Exploratory Data Analysis differ from Classical Data Analysis?
sourceRecords.notes: Read live 2026-08-21. Contrasts the classical sequence (Problem, Data, Model, Analysis, Conclusions) with the EDA sequence (Problem, Data, Analysis, Model, Conclusions): EDA analyzes immediately after collection with the goal of inferring what model would be appropriate. Supports the explore-before-modeling principle and the exploration-vs-confirmation contrast.

sourceRecords.title: NIST/SEMATECH e-Handbook of Statistical Methods — 1.1.4. What are the EDA Goals?
sourceRecords.notes: Read live 2026-08-21. States the primary goal of EDA is maximizing the analyst's insight into a dataset and its underlying structure, and that insight means detecting and uncovering structure and knowing what is not in the data. Supports the goals section.

sourceRecords.title: NIST/SEMATECH e-Handbook of Statistical Methods — 1.3.2. Analysis Questions
sourceRecords.notes: Read live 2026-08-21. Lists common EDA questions including 'what is a typical value?', spread/distribution questions, and whether variables relate; notes the scatter plot is broad-brushed and applies almost universally, and that EDA emphasizes graphical techniques for gaining insight. Supports the typical-value/spread claims and the scatter-plot naming.

sourceRecords.title: NIST/SEMATECH e-Handbook of Statistical Methods — 1.1.5. The Role of Graphics
sourceRecords.notes: Read live 2026-08-21. Lists scatter plots, histograms, and box plots among graphical techniques and states the EDA approach relies heavily on them as the shortest path to gaining insight into a dataset. Supports the charts-as-tools claim.

sourceRecords.title: Tukey, John W. — 'We Need Both Exploratory and Confirmatory', The American Statistician, Vol. 34, No. 1 (1980), pp. 23-25
sourceRecords.notes: Taylor & Francis live page is bot-blocked; the abstract was read via an Internet Archive capture of the canonical URL (web.archive.org snapshot 2025-12-14). Abstract states: ideas come from previous exploration more often than from lightning strokes; finding the question is often more important than finding the answer; EDA is an attitude, a flexibility, and a reliance on display, NOT a bundle of techniques; we need both exploratory and confirmatory analysis; be prepared to randomize and avoid multiplicity. Supports the attitude framing, the hypothesis-finding role of exploration, and the anti-cherry-picking honesty principle.

sourceRecords.title: Introduction to Modern Statistics (2nd ed.), Chapter 5: Exploring numerical data
sourceRecords.notes: Read live 2026-08-21. Chapter focuses on exploring numerical data using summary statistics and visualizations; covers dot plots and the mean, histograms and shape, variance and standard deviation, box plots, quartiles, and the median; box-plot whiskers reach to the minimum and maximum values; median and IQR are robust where the mean and standard deviation are not. Supports the summary-numbers (min, max, mean, median, spread) and distribution-chart claims.
